explanation: `git push` sends commit objects to the remote server.
Sets upstream tracking. Once set, you can just type `git push` or `git pull`.
tip: Check tracking branches anytime with `git branch -vv`.

explanation: Cloning downloads all commits, branches, and tags.
tip: You do NOT need to run `git init` before `git clone` — clone does it for you!

explanation: Fetch inspects; pull merges. Fetch never touches your working files.
tip: If unsure, run `git fetch` first and inspect with `git log origin/main`.

explanation: `git pull` literally combines fetch and merge into one operation.
tip: You can also configure `git pull --rebase` to keep a linear history.

explanation: Non-fast-forward means your local branch is behind the remote.
tip: Pull first, merge or rebase, then push.

explanation: Standard workflow: Pull down changes, test locally, push back up.
tip: This is the core cadence of modern team programming.

explanation: Example: `git clone https://... .` clones directly into the current directory.
tip: Useful when you already created an empty project folder.

explanation: Pull early and often to keep conflicts small and manageable.
tip: Make 'git pull' your morning coffee routine.

explanation: Force pushing rewrites remote history. Always use `--force-with-lease` if you must force push your own feature branch.
tip: Most professional repositories enable branch protection to block force pushes on main.
